newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Buyers boot Australian stocks to higher close.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Buyers boot Australian stocks to higher close.

text.p: SPI futures 2439 +14 US 30yr cl 6.79 +0.01
10yrbond futs 92.335 +0.015 Gold NY 358.85 Lon fix 359.00
*Stocks end higher as investors go shopping, rate cut talk prompts mid-afternoon spurt. Volume 360.17 million, value A$661.5 million, 1,080 stocks traded, 331 steady, 426 rises, 323 falls.

The Australian share market closed higher on Wednesday as buyers, buoyed by a resilient performance from Wall Street, jumped into a market that was seen becoming increasingly comfortable with its higher levels of late.
At 4.10 p.m. (0510 GMT), the All Ordinaries index was 14.3 points higher at 2,415.0. March share price index futures were up 14 points at 2,439, a 24.0 point premium to the index.

A frisson of excitement hit the market in mid-afternoon as loose talk of a Reserve Bank interest rate cut saw the benchmark spike six points to its day high. The talk died just as quickly though and the market settled back into its comfort zone.

"The talk after lunch was that weak retail sales gave them an excuse to cut rates but we didn't hold much by it," said a Sydney-based dealer, adding that the market was overbought at the day's higher levels.
"The last cut still has to work its way through and at those (higher) levels the market was overdone," the broker said.
"The rate cut talk gave it a nudge along," said broker Justin Hondris of Hartley Poynton, adding that the bullion price may have steadied, it could be only temporary.
"Gold is still looking very average. Any buying that is coming in, people are jumping on it to sell," he said.
Hondris pointed to continuing interest in the second tier oil producers as investors looked for exposure to the currently fashionable sector.
"Some of smaller stocks like Omega Oil, Bligh Oil and Tap Oil are running," he said. All three mid-size oils were active, each seeing over two million shares traded on the day.

In the resource leaders, gold/nickel miner WMC impressed, finding substantial buying interest at its lower levels. "It was always going to get support around the A$7.70 level," said one trader, citing the miners low point for the year so far.

In the industrials, the retail sector continued to feature with electrical and furniture retailer, Harvey Norman, sounding the now familiar refrain of a depressed retail sector. The company's shares ended four percent lower at A$6.15, albeit on very light trade.
Other retailers to suffer on the day included apparel retailers, Country Road and Just Jeans. Both companies reported 50 percent profit downgrades after the market closed on Tuesday.
Country Road shares closed 17 percent lower at A$1.40 while Just Jeans scrip lost 8 percent to A$1.65 in very thin trade.
Rises outnumbered falls by a ratio of about nine to seven, while about 31 percent of stocks traded remained steady.
FUTURES/OPTIONS - Derivatives trade was little changed from Tuesday's moderate levels.
Total options traded 34,353 (33,338)
Turnover in March SPI contracts totalled 5,197 (5,973)

In other local markets, short-dated Australian bond and bill futures remained firm amid cautious optimism of a further cut in official interest rates before the end of the quarter, and there had even been speculation about an easing today. By 5.00 p.m. (0600 GMT), 10 year T-bonds had edged down to 7.54 percent.

The Australian dollar sagged to its lowest local close in two months Wednesday as a rampant rumour mill chewed up support. Traders said some real selling of AUD/yen was seen out of Tokyo but most of the fall was due to far-fetched speculation about an imminent cut in official cash rates. The talk actually grew clamorous enough to draw a rare official denial from the Reserve Bank, but the damage had been done and the dollar needed local exporters' bids to prevent a test of US$0.7850 support.
By 5.15 p.m. (0615 GMT), the unit had been harried to US$0.7875/80, its lowest local close since November 8, from an early US$0.7900/05 and US$0.7903/08 late here Tuesday.
